headline: Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade Hits 100 (Give or Take a Couple of Days)

paragraphs.text: It was a centennial celebration 102 years, and two days, in the making.

The Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, a mainstay of the holiday, set off under a bluish sky Saturday for the 100th time in its history — and for the first time on a day other than Thanksgiving, after weather delayed the event by two days.

The event was postponed late on Wednesday after forecasters predicted extreme winds and inclement weather in New York City, upending plans for thousands of would-be spectators, visitors and performers.
The decision was among only a handful of occasions when the procession’s schedule has been altered, chief among them World War II, when a helium shortage led to a three-year hiatus.

But on Saturday, the rescheduled parade went off with few hitches, as hundreds of thousands of people thronged the sidewalks of Upper and Midtown Manhattan to catch a glimpse of glittering floats and bobbing balloons, and many more tuned in to the broadcast at home.

The scene was somewhat mellower than past years, some spectators said, as the festivities coincided with holiday shopping and long weekend sojourns. Still, the sidewalks bustled from early morning till noon as the parade snaked its way down the center of Manhattan.

There was Gloria Gaynor, JoJo and the casts of several hit Broadway shows belting songs and twirling along. There were youth marching bands, who remained in the city against the odds, tooting horns and clapping cymbals. And there was Smash Mouth, Baha Men and the Indigo Girls, playing their hits to elated crowds as Pikachu, Smokey Bear and Snoopy soared overhead.

By the end, the parade showcased some 30 giant balloons, 28 floats, eight marching bands and dozens of performers, Macy’s said, though at least a few groups originally scheduled to perform, including the University of Alabama’s marching band and Macy’s Great American Marching Band were forced to skip their shows after the delay.
For others, though, the Saturday step-off afforded the chance of a lifetime: a front-row seat to the parade’s 100th procession.
“It feels festive in a more general way,” said Destinee Filmore, who came to the parade route from Harlem because of the delay. “It feels more like a holiday.”
Nate Schweber, Miles G. Cohen, Sarah Maslin Nir and Mack Liederman contributed reporting.
